summary: Documents an existing, widely used protocol and common implementation: BSD rlogin. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets you sit at one computer and type on another.

why is rlogin trusted host login risky
subtitle: How the BSD remote-login protocol sets up a session over TCP port 513, and the security risk of its trusted-host shortcut.

tldr.problem: Unix users wanted remote login that carried more of the Unix terminal environment than Telnet does, and without typing a password when connecting from trusted hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TCP connection to port 513 and sends four null-terminated strings. The server then streams data and uses TCP urgent data to send single-byte control messages.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents an existing, widely used protocol and is not an Internet standard. It warns that password-free login from trusted hosts weakens security.

today: RFC 1282 is Informational and documents an existing protocol; it does not specify an Internet standard. It obsoleted RFC 1258, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Rlogin Provides
sections.content:
The rlogin facility provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal with proper flushing of output. It is widely used between Unix hosts because it carries more of the Unix terminal environment semantics than the Telnet protocol, and because on many Unix hosts it can be configured not to ask for a password when connections come from trusted hosts.

It requires TCP, uses contact port 513 and assumes an eight-bit transparent stream. This memo obsoletes RFC 1258 and describes an existing protocol and common implementation rather than a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Rlogin is a way to use a faraway computer from your keyboard. It rides on TCP and listens at door number 513.

sections.title: Setting Up and Closing a Session
sections.content:
After the connection is established, the client sends four null-terminated strings: an empty string (a single zero byte), the client username, the server username, and the terminal type and speed, such as vt100/9600. The server replies with a zero byte to say it has them and is now in data transfer mode. Window size negotiation may follow.

When the TCP connection closes in either direction, the side that notices should shut down in an orderly way, restoring terminal modes and notifying the user or processes before closing the other direction.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first says who is calling, who they want to be, and what kind of screen they have. The server answers with a single zero byte meaning ready.

sections.title: Data, Flow Control and Window Size
sections.content:
The client starts in cooked mode, where it intercepts the START and STOP characters (usually ASCII DC1 and DC3) to start and stop output. In raw mode they are sent to the server as ordinary characters. The server marks control messages by placing a single control byte in the data stream and pointing the TCP urgent-data pointer at it. Hex 02 discards unwritten buffered output, 10 switches the client to raw mode, 20 resumes local START and STOP handling, and 80 asks the client to send its window size. Other values are ignored, and the control byte is never shown to the user.

When the client's window changes, it sends a 12-byte sequence: two bytes of hex FF as a magic cookie, two lower-case ASCII s bytes, then four 16-bit values in network byte order for rows, columns, and pixels in X and Y.

The client also has an escape character, customarily the tilde, handled specially only at the beginning of a line. The escape followed by a dot, or by the end-of-file character, closes the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can slip in secret one-byte notes to tell the screen to stop, go or clear. When your window is resized, the client sends a short message with the new size.

sections.title: A Cautionary Tale
sections.content:
Letting a user set up trusted users or hosts that can log in without a password is convenient, but the memo says it weakens security and has been exploited in previous attacks. Passwordless login among all your systems means one compromised system can open all the others. A suggested compromise is to allow bypass from only one workstation to the other systems.

Trusted hosts are ordinarily specified by name, so compromising a domain name server or the network could let an untrusted host pose as a trusted one. A trusted-logins file left writeable by others can also be altered. The memo says secure authentication extensions such as Kerberos can reduce these risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the password is like leaving a spare key under the mat for all your friends' houses. If a burglar finds one key, they can open every door.
